history.heading: Ancient China
paragraphs: China is one of the world's oldest civilisations. Neolithic cultures grew millet and rice along the Yellow and Yangtze rivers thousands of years ago. The Shang dynasty (around 1600–1046 BCE) left the earliest Chinese writing on oracle bones. Under the Zhou dynasty, Confucius and Laozi founded philosophical traditions that shaped East Asian culture.

In 221 BCE Qin Shi Huang unified China as its first emperor, standardising writing, currency and measurements; his tomb is guarded by the Terracotta Army. The Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE) expanded the empire, opened the Silk Road and gave its name to the majority Han Chinese.

history.heading: Imperial dynasties
paragraphs: Periods of unity and division alternated over two thousand years. The Tang dynasty (618–907) was a golden age of poetry and cosmopolitan culture, and the Song dynasty (960–1279) saw remarkable advances in technology, commerce and the arts. Chinese inventions such as paper, printing, the compass and gunpowder spread to the rest of the world.

The Mongols ruled China as the Yuan dynasty, followed by the Ming dynasty, which built much of the Great Wall as it stands today and sent the fleets of Zheng He across the Indian Ocean. The Manchu Qing dynasty, from 1644, expanded China to its largest extent.

history.heading: Century of humiliation and revolution
paragraphs: In the 19th century the Qing were weakened by internal rebellions, such as the Taiping Rebellion, which killed tens of millions, and by Western powers and Japan, which defeated China in wars, including the Opium Wars, and forced unequal treaties. Hong Kong was ceded to Britain.

The 1911 revolution ended imperial rule, and the Republic of China was founded in 1912. Warlordism, civil war between the Nationalists (Kuomintang) and the Communists, and a brutal Japanese invasion from 1937 followed. In 1949 the Communists under Mao Zedong won the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, while the Nationalists retreated to Taiwan.

history.heading: The People's Republic
paragraphs: Mao's rule included the Great Leap Forward (1958–62), which caused a famine that killed tens of millions, and the Cultural Revolution (1966–76), a decade of political violence. After Mao's death, Deng Xiaoping launched "reform and opening up" from 1978, introducing market reforms that produced decades of rapid growth and lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty.

Political liberalisation did not follow: the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests were crushed by the army. China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, hosted the 2008 Olympics, and has become a global superpower. Since 2012, Xi Jinping has centralised power, with term limits on the presidency removed in 2018.

culture.heading: Language and philosophy
paragraphs: Standard Chinese (Mandarin) is the official language, and many other Chinese languages such as Cantonese, Wu and Min are spoken, all sharing a writing system of characters; simplified characters are used in mainland China. China officially recognises 56 ethnic groups; the Han are about 91 percent, with minorities including Zhuang, Uyghurs, Hui, Tibetans and Mongols.
Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism have deeply shaped Chinese values, such as respect for family and education. Officially the state is atheist, and religious activity is regulated.

culture.heading: Arts and festivals
paragraphs: Chinese culture includes calligraphy, ink painting, porcelain, silk, classical poetry and opera, including Peking opera. The Four Great Classical Novels, such as Journey to the West, are widely known. Modern Chinese cinema, literature and video games have growing global audiences.

The Spring Festival (Chinese New Year) is the most important holiday, with family reunions and the largest annual human migration on Earth. The Mid-Autumn Festival and Dragon Boat Festival are also major celebrations.

culture.heading: Food and sport
paragraphs: Chinese cuisine is famously diverse, with regional styles such as Sichuan, Cantonese, Shandong and Hunan. Dishes include Peking duck, dumplings, hot pot, noodles and dim sum. Tea culture has a history of thousands of years.
Table tennis, badminton, basketball and martial arts such as kung fu and tai chi are popular. China hosted the Summer Olympics in 2008 and the Winter Olympics in 2022.

politics.heading: One-party state
paragraphs: The People's Republic of China is a one-party state led by the Chinese Communist Party. Real power rests with the party's top leadership, especially the Politburo Standing Committee and the General Secretary, who is also president and chairman of the Central Military Commission. The National People's Congress is formally the highest state body.

Hong Kong and Macau are special administrative regions under the "one country, two systems" principle, though Beijing has tightened control over Hong Kong since 2020. Human rights groups and many governments criticise repression in Xinjiang and Tibet, censorship and the treatment of dissidents.

politics.heading: Global power
paragraphs: China is a permanent member of the UN Security Council and has the world's largest navy by number of ships. Its Belt and Road Initiative finances infrastructure in many countries. It claims Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out the use of force, and it has disputes over islands and waters in the South China Sea and East China Sea.
Relations with the United States combine deep economic interdependence with strategic rivalry over trade, technology and security.

economy.heading: The world's factory
paragraphs: China has the world's second-largest economy by nominal GDP and the largest by purchasing power. It is the largest manufacturer and exporter, producing everything from clothing and electronics to steel, ships, solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles, in which it has become the global leader.

Its growth was driven by exports, investment and urbanisation. Chinese technology companies such as Huawei, Alibaba, Tencent, BYD and DeepSeek have become globally significant. The currency is the renminbi (yuan).

economy.heading: New challenges
paragraphs: Growth has slowed. China faces a prolonged property sector downturn, local government debt, weak consumer demand, youth unemployment and a shrinking, ageing population. Trade tensions with the United States and Europe have increased, and the government is prioritising self-reliance in advanced technologies such as semiconductors.
China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases but also the largest investor in renewable energy.
